concepts.title: @SpringBootTest and Test Slices
concepts.description: @SpringBootTest boots the entire ApplicationContext for a true end-to-end test, while test slices like @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest load only the beans one layer needs. The trade-off between fidelity and speed shapes how a healthy Spring Boot test suite is structured.
learningObjectives: Explain what @SpringBootTest does and when a genuine full-context integration test is actually justified.
Explain what a test slice is and describe what @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest each load and exclude.
Explain, mechanistically, why test slices start dramatically faster than @SpringBootTest.
Predict which beans are and are not available inside a given test slice, and what happens when you autowire a bean that isn't.
Choose the appropriate test annotation -- plain unit test, a specific slice, or full @SpringBootTest -- for a given testing scenario.

sections.heading: The Cost of a Full ApplicationContext in Tests
sections.body:
`@SpringBootTest` on a test class tells Spring Boot to do what it does when your application runs in production: build a complete `ApplicationContext`, run component scanning across your whole base package, evaluate every autoconfiguration condition, and construct every bean your application defines (controllers, services, repositories, the lot). With `webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT` it goes further and starts a real embedded servlet container on a randomly chosen TCP port, so a test can send genuine HTTP requests to it, the way a real client would. The default, `WebEnvironment.MOCK`, builds the same full context but serves requests through a mock servlet environment with no real port.

That fidelity has a price. Every bean in the graph has to be instantiated and wired, every autoconfiguration class runs its conditional checks, and if the application talks to a real (or embedded) database, that connection has to be established. A small application may need a second or two; a production-sized codebase with dozens of services, repositories and autoconfigured integrations can take several seconds to boot a single `@SpringBootTest` context, before the test has asserted anything. Multiply that by hundreds of test classes that each need their own context, and a suite that should finish in under a minute can turn into a ten- or fifteen-minute wait. That recurring pain is why test slices exist.

sections.heading: Test Slices: Loading Only What You Need
sections.body:
A **test slice** is a test annotation that boots a deliberately restricted subset of the autoconfiguration and component-scanning machinery: just enough to exercise one architectural layer in isolation.

`@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)` loads the web layer only: `DispatcherServlet`, `HandlerMapping`, the registered `HttpMessageConverter`s (Jackson among them), `@ControllerAdvice` beans, Bean Validation support, and the controller class you named (or every `@Controller`/`@RestController` in the base package, if you omit the argument). It does **not** component-scan your `@Service` or `@Repository` beans. If `OrderController` depends on an `OrderService`, that dependency is not satisfied automatically, and you must supply a test double yourself (typically with `@MockBean`, covered later in this module). The restriction is intentional: a controller test verifies routing, request and response binding, and validation, not a real service and a real database as well.

`@DataJpaTest` is the mirror image for the persistence layer. It configures an embedded, in-memory database (H2 by default, if it is on the classpath) instead of your production datasource, scans for `@Entity` classes and Spring Data repository interfaces, and wires up a real `EntityManager`, but registers none of your `@Service` or `@Controller` beans. It also wraps every test method in a transaction that is rolled back at the end of the method, so tests never leak data into one another and need no cleanup code (the examples below show this).

sections.heading: Why Slices Load Faster: Fewer Beans, and Context Caching
sections.body:
The speed difference between a slice and a full `@SpringBootTest` comes from two effects. First, there are far fewer beans to construct: a `@WebMvcTest` for one controller might build a few dozen beans, while the full context of a real application might build several hundred. Fewer beans means less reflection-based construction, less dependency-graph resolution, and no attempt to open a database connection unless the slice needs one.

Second, Spring's test framework **caches contexts across test classes**. If two test classes request a context built from the same configuration (the same slice annotation, the same set of `@MockBean`s, the same active profiles), Spring reuses the context built for the first instead of building another. A slice's configuration is narrow and easy to keep identical across many test classes, so many `@WebMvcTest` classes in a codebase share one cache key. `@SpringBootTest` classes are more likely to differ in a profile or a set of mocked beans, which forces a new context each time and defeats the cache. `@DirtiesContext` opts a test out of the cache by forcing the context to be discarded and rebuilt after that test. It is useful when a test mutates shared singleton state in a way that would corrupt later tests, but it brings back the startup cost the cache exists to avoid, so use it sparingly. Resetting the state some other way (a cleanup step, or a mock that is reset between tests) usually costs less than rebuilding the context.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Tool: Plain Unit Test, Slice, or Full Context
sections.body:
A healthy test suite is a mix, chosen per test's purpose. For pure business logic with no Spring dependency (a pricing calculation, a validation rule written as a plain method), a plain JUnit test with `new SomeClass()` and, if needed, hand-written or Mockito-created fakes needs no Spring context and runs in milliseconds. For checking that one layer's Spring-specific wiring works (does this controller route requests and bind JSON the way I expect? does this repository's derived query produce the right SQL?), a test slice is the right level: it exercises real Spring infrastructure for the layer under test, with everything else mocked or absent. `@SpringBootTest` earns its cost for end-to-end scenarios: a request flowing from the controller through a real service into a real (often Testcontainers-backed) database and back, as it would in production.

The common mistake is reaching for `@SpringBootTest` out of habit for every test, including ones that touch only one layer. The test passes, but it taxes the whole suite's runtime for nothing the test is actually verifying, and the cost grows with every test class that makes the same choice. The question to ask is not 'will this work?' but 'does this test need more than one layer wired together to make its assertion meaningful?'

examples.title: @WebMvcTest: Web Layer Only, With a Mocked Service
examples.explanation: @WebMvcTest(OrderController.class) restricts the context to the web layer and this one controller. DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, Jackson's HttpMessageConverter and validation support are present, but no @Service or @Repository bean is component-scanned into the context. Because OrderController's constructor requires an OrderService, the test has to supply one: @MockBean registers a Mockito mock of OrderService in this narrow context so the controller can be constructed. The test never touches a real service or database. It verifies that a GET to this URL is routed correctly and that the returned Order is serialized to the expected JSON.

examples.title: @DataJpaTest: Persistence Layer Only, With Automatic Rollback
examples.explanation: @DataJpaTest swaps in an embedded, in-memory database instead of the application's real datasource and registers only @Entity classes and Spring Data repository interfaces, so no @Service or @Controller beans exist in this context. TestEntityManager is a test-oriented wrapper Spring Boot provides for this slice. It lets the test persist data directly, bypassing the repository under test, so the setup doesn't depend on the method being tested. The second test shows the rollback: @DataJpaTest wraps every test method in its own transaction and rolls it back at the end, so the two orders persisted in the first test are gone when the second runs, with no cleanup code.

examples.title: @SpringBootTest With a Real Embedded Server: True End-to-End
examples.explanation: Unlike the two slice examples, this test builds the ENTIRE application context (every controller, service and repository) plus a real embedded servlet container on a random port, and TestRestTemplate sends genuine HTTP requests to it, as an external client would. It is the only one of the three examples that proves the controller, service and repository cooperate end to end, including real HTTP serialization on both sides, and it is by a wide margin the slowest to start, since nothing is restricted or mocked. Using this style for every test, instead of reserving it for cross-layer scenarios, is the habit that makes large Spring Boot suites slow. Two practical notes. First, the server handles each request on its own thread, outside the test's transaction, so data created through these calls is committed and is not rolled back after the test, unlike in @DataJpaTest. Second, in Spring Boot 4 @SpringBootTest no longer provides a TestRestTemplate bean automatically: you add @AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate and the spring-boot-resttestclient dependency (the class moves to org.springframework.boot.resttestclient).

misconceptions.description: @WebMvcTest loads the entire application, just with a mock server instead of a real one listening on a port.
misconceptions.clarification: @WebMvcTest restricts which BEANS get loaded, not just how the server is exposed: it excludes @Service and @Repository component scanning, along with most autoconfiguration unrelated to the web layer. A controller's non-web dependencies (typically a service) are absent from this context unless you supply them, most often with @MockBean. This differs from @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = MOCK), which DOES build the full application context, every bean your app defines, but serves requests through a mock servlet environment instead of a real network port. The two axes, which beans are loaded and whether a real socket is opened, are independent.
misconceptions.fact: @WebMvcTest restricts which beans get loaded, not just how the server is exposed: it excludes @Service and @Repository component scanning, along with most autoconfiguration unrelated to the web layer.

misconceptions.description: Since @DataJpaTest starts a real repository bean backed by a real EntityManager, it must be exercising the exact same database and configuration the production application uses.
misconceptions.clarification: @DataJpaTest replaces your production datasource configuration with an embedded, in-memory database (H2 by default, when it is on the classpath) for the duration of the test, and wraps every test method in a transaction that is rolled back when the method finishes. The repository and EntityManager are real Spring Data / JPA objects running real SQL, but the database is a disposable stand-in, not your production database or even a persistent local one, and nothing written during a test is retained. That is what makes @DataJpaTest fast and safe to run repeatedly with no cleanup. The trade-off is that H2 is not your production database: SQL dialect differences, native queries and database-specific column types can behave differently there. When that matters, add @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE) and point the test at a real database, commonly a Testcontainers one.

exercises.prompt: This @WebMvcTest fails at startup with 'NoSuchBeanDefinitionException: No qualifying bean of type OrderService available.' Find and fix the bug so the test can construct OrderController successfully.
hints: @WebMvcTest deliberately does NOT perform full component scanning -- does it register @Service beans like OrderService into the context at all?
@Autowired only finds a bean that already exists in the context. If no OrderService bean was ever registered here, what should happen instead of trying to autowire a real one?
You need a way to supply a stand-in OrderService so OrderController's constructor can be satisfied, without loading the real service bean at all.
exercises.solutionExplanation: @WebMvcTest scans and registers only the web layer (@Controller/@RestController beans plus supporting web infrastructure) and excludes @Service and @Repository beans from component scanning. No OrderService bean exists in this context, so @Autowired has nothing to find, and the context fails to start while constructing OrderController, whose constructor demands an OrderService. Replacing @Autowired with @MockBean fixes it: instead of looking for an existing bean, @MockBean creates a Mockito mock and registers it as the OrderService bean in this test's context, which satisfies OrderController's constructor and keeps the real service, and everything it depends on, out of the picture.

exercises.prompt: Given this @DataJpaTest class with two test methods, what does each assertion produce, and why doesn't the second test see the order persisted by the first?
hints: @DataJpaTest wraps every test method in its own transaction by default -- what happens to that transaction once the test method finishes?
JUnit doesn't reset database state between methods for you. What mechanism resets things between these two?
Neither test method contains any manual cleanup code (no @AfterEach deleting rows) -- so the reset has to be happening automatically, at the transaction level.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Both assertions pass: firstTestPersistsAnItem sees count() == 1 right after persisting one item, and secondTestSeesAnEmptyTable sees count() == 0, because @DataJpaTest automatically rolls back each test method's transaction once that method completes -- the widget persisted in the first test never actually commits, so the second test starts from a genuinely empty table.
exercises.solutionExplanation: @DataJpaTest wraps every test method in its own database transaction and, by default, rolls it back when the method finishes, whether the test passed or failed. In firstTestPersistsAnItem, entityManager.persist(...) adds a row within that transaction, so inventoryRepository.count() reports 1 while still inside it. When the method returns, Spring's test framework rolls the transaction back and the insert disappears. secondTestSeesAnEmptyTable runs in a new transaction that knows nothing of the first test's data, so count() reports 0. This automatic rollback is why @DataJpaTest tests can run in any order and be repeated without teardown code.

assessments.prompt: Which of the following best explains why a @WebMvcTest-based test suite typically starts dramatically faster than the equivalent @SpringBootTest-based suite?
options: @WebMvcTest tests run in a separate, permanently pre-warmed JVM that Spring Boot maintains between test runs.

@WebMvcTest loads a deliberately restricted set of beans (the web layer only, excluding @Service/@Repository component scanning), and its narrow, easily-repeated configuration also benefits more consistently from Spring's test-context caching.
@WebMvcTest disables Jackson's JSON serialization, so responses are returned as plain text instead, which is faster to produce.
@WebMvcTest skips Bean Validation entirely, which is the single largest cost in a typical Spring Boot context startup.
assessments.explanation: The speed advantage has two sources: far fewer beans need to be constructed (no full component scan for services and repositories, no autoconfiguration unrelated to the web layer), and a slice's narrow, easily kept-identical configuration is reused across test classes through Spring's test-context caching more often than a typical @SpringBootTest configuration, which tends to vary just enough between test classes to force a fresh context. The “@WebMvcTest disables Jackson's JSON serialization, so responses…” option is false: Jackson-based JSON conversion stays active in @WebMvcTest. The “@WebMvcTest tests run in a separate, permanently…” option describes a JVM-level mechanism Spring Boot does not have. The “@WebMvcTest skips Bean Validation entirely…” option is false: Bean Validation is present in @WebMvcTest and isn't the dominant cost of a full context startup anyway.

assessments.prompt: A @DataJpaTest class autowires a real OrderRepository and asserts against data it persists via TestEntityManager. Which statement about this test is accurate?
options: It requires explicit cleanup code (an @AfterEach deleting rows) at the end of each test method, or later tests will see leftover data from earlier ones.
It also loads and exercises any @Service or @Controller beans that happen to depend on OrderRepository.
It exercises a genuine Spring Data JPA repository and EntityManager.
It exercises the exact same database configuration -- URL, driver, and data -- that the production application actually connects to.
assessments.explanation: @DataJpaTest deliberately swaps in an embedded, in-memory database in place of the production datasource, and wraps every test method in its own transaction that's automatically rolled back afterward -- the repository and EntityManager objects themselves are genuinely real, but the database backing them is a disposable stand-in. The “It exercises the exact same database configuration…” option is exactly the misconception this concept calls out directly. The “It requires explicit cleanup code…” option is wrong because the automatic rollback IS the cleanup mechanism -- no manual teardown code is needed. The “It also loads and exercises any @Service…” option is wrong -- @DataJpaTest registers only @Entity classes and repository interfaces, explicitly excluding @Service and @Controller beans from its restricted context.

assessments.prompt: A test class is annotated @DirtiesContext, applied after a test that mutates a shared singleton bean's internal state in a way that would corrupt later tests. What is the direct effect of this annotation?
options: It forces Spring's test framework to discard the cached ApplicationContext after this test runs and build a fresh one the next time a context is needed, at the cost of reintroducing that context's full startup time.
It marks the test as flaky so the CI pipeline automatically retries it on failure.
It prevents the test's own transaction from being rolled back at the end of the method.
It disables all @MockBean stubbing within this specific test class from that point forward.
assessments.explanation: @DirtiesContext opts a test out of Spring's test-context caching by forcing the context to be discarded and rebuilt afterward. It is useful when a test has mutated shared singleton state in a way that would corrupt later tests reusing the same cached context, but it brings back the startup cost the cache exists to avoid, which is why it should be used sparingly. The “It marks the test as flaky…”, “It disables all @MockBean stubbing within…” and “It prevents the test's own transaction…” options each describe an effect @DirtiesContext does not have: it has nothing to do with retries, mock stubbing or transaction rollback.

assessments.prompt: A class PricingCalculator has no Spring annotations at all and depends on nothing but plain Java objects passed into its constructor. According to this module's guidance on choosing a testing approach, what is the most appropriate way to test it?
options: @WebMvcTest, scoped narrowly to just this one class.
@DataJpaTest, since among Spring's test annotations it boots the fastest.
@SpringBootTest, since every class in a Spring Boot codebase should be tested against the full application context for consistency.
A plain JUnit test that constructs PricingCalculator directly with `new`, using hand-written or Mockito-created fakes for any collaborators if needed -- no Spring context of any kind is required.
assessments.explanation: Pure business logic with no Spring dependency needs no Spring context. A plain JUnit test with `new` and, if needed, a hand-written or Mockito-created fake runs in milliseconds and is the proportionate tool here. The “@SpringBootTest, since every class in a Spring…” option describes the habit named earlier as a common mistake: reaching for @SpringBootTest by default instead of asking whether the test needs more than one layer wired together. The “@DataJpaTest, since among Spring's test annotations…” and “@WebMvcTest, scoped narrowly to just this one class” options both bring in Spring test infrastructure (an embedded database and the web layer) that PricingCalculator has no relationship to.

assessments.prompt: A teammate wants to write every single test in the codebase using @SpringBootTest 'to be safe.' Explain the trade-off they're making, and describe when a test slice or a plain unit test would be the better choice instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: @SpringBootTest builds the same full ApplicationContext the real application uses in production: every controller, service, repository and autoconfigured bean, plus, with a real webEnvironment, an embedded server on a real port. That gives the highest fidelity, since the test exercises the application's whole wiring. The cost is that every one of those beans must be constructed and wired for each test class that needs a distinct context configuration, which in a real-sized application can mean several seconds per class and minutes of overhead across a large suite before a single assertion has run. 'To be safe' conflates two questions: whether a test COULD catch a bug (true of almost any test that runs the relevant code) and whether it NEEDS the fully wired application to make its assertion meaningful. A test asserting that a controller routes a GET request and serializes the response as JSON doesn't need a real service or database. A @WebMvcTest with the service mocked via @MockBean verifies the same routing and serialization with a fraction of the beans, and it benefits more reliably from context caching because its configuration tends to stay identical from one test class to the next. A test of pure business logic, such as a discount calculation, needs no Spring context at all: a plain JUnit test with `new` and, if needed, a hand-written fake runs in milliseconds. The healthiest suite reserves @SpringBootTest for the comparatively rare tests about cross-layer integration (does a request flow correctly from the controller through a real service into a real or embedded database and back?) and uses slices or plain unit tests for everything that exercises one layer or no Spring machinery.

concepts.title: Testing Controllers with MockMvc
concepts.description: MockMvc simulates HTTP requests against Spring MVC's real dispatch machinery without opening an actual network socket, letting you assert on status codes, headers, and JSON response bodies with precision, at unit-test speed.
learningObjectives: Explain what MockMvc actually does and how it differs from firing real HTTP requests at a running server.
Perform a GET or POST request through MockMvc and assert on status code, content type, and JSON body fields using jsonPath.
Explain how MockMvc becomes available inside a @WebMvcTest, and how it can also be obtained in a full @SpringBootTest.
Chain multiple andExpect() assertions and explain what happens, and what gets reported, when one of them fails.
Explain why a MockMvc test still meaningfully exercises real Spring MVC infrastructure -- routing, converters, and validation -- despite never opening a socket.

sections.heading: What MockMvc Actually Does
sections.body:
`MockMvc` is a Spring test utility that simulates an HTTP request dispatched through Spring MVC's real machinery (`DispatcherServlet`, `HandlerMapping`, argument resolvers, `HttpMessageConverter`s and any registered `@ExceptionHandler`s) entirely in memory, with no servlet container and no TCP socket. That is a different tool from `TestRestTemplate` or `WebTestClient`, which send genuine HTTP requests to a real, running server (typically with `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)`, as in the previous concept) and so test the whole stack including real network serialization. MockMvc tests the web layer's *logic* (routing, binding, conversion, validation, error handling) without a network round trip.

The word 'mock' here means something slightly different than in `@MockBean` or plain Mockito. It doesn't mean 'a fake stand-in that returns whatever you told it to.' It means 'a simulated request/response exchange that never touches a socket', and the request-handling code itself is real.

sections.heading: Building and Performing Requests
sections.body:
A typical MockMvc test builds a request using static methods from `MockMvcRequestBuilders` (`get(...)`, `post(...)`, `put(...)`, `delete(...)`), optionally attaches a body and a `Content-Type` for write operations, calls `perform(...)`, and then chains one or more `andExpect(...)` assertions against the resulting `ResultActions`:

```java
mockMvc.perform(get("/api/orders/1"))
        .andExpect(status().isOk())
        .andExpect(content().contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
        .andExpect(jsonPath("$.customerName").value("Amy"))
        .andExpect(jsonPath("$.items", hasSize(2)));
```

`jsonPath("$.customerName")` navigates the response body as parsed JSON, using a JSONPath expression -- `$` is the document root, `.customerName` descends into that field, `$.items[0]` would index into an array's first element, and `hasSize(2)` (a Hamcrest matcher) asserts an array's length directly rather than its contents. For a write operation, the request body is typically built by serializing a Java object with an `ObjectMapper` and attaching it explicitly:

```java
mockMvc.perform(post("/api/orders")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content(objectMapper.writeValueAsString(request)))
        .andExpect(status().isCreated());
```

sections.heading: Why It's Still a Real Test of Your Web Layer
sections.body:
Nothing about Spring MVC's own components is replaced with a fake, which is a common point of confusion. The real `DispatcherServlet` dispatches the request; the real `HandlerMapping` picks the controller method; real argument resolvers bind `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam` and `@RequestBody` parameters as they would for a genuine HTTP request; the autoconfigured Jackson `HttpMessageConverter` does the JSON serialization and deserialization; Bean Validation runs against `@Valid` parameters; and any `@RestControllerAdvice` you've registered handles thrown exceptions as it would in production. Only the transport layer is simulated: no socket, no servlet container thread pool, no network latency. From the moment the request 'arrives' onward, it is the production code path.

That is why a MockMvc test catches real bugs: a typo in a `@RequestMapping` path, a missing `@Valid`, a controller returning the wrong HTTP status, a validation constraint that doesn't fire as you expect. The code responsible for each of them is running, not stubbed out.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls: Content-Type, JSON Path Syntax, and Assertion Failures
sections.body:
The most common mistake when POSTing a body through MockMvc is forgetting `.contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)` on the request. Without it, Spring MVC has no declared `Content-Type` to choose a message converter by (the default is `application/octet-stream`), a `@RequestBody` parameter can't be bound, and the response is a `415 Unsupported Media Type` that has nothing to do with your business logic or the shape of your JSON.

A second source of friction is JSONPath mistakes. `jsonPath("$.items[0].name")` and `jsonPath("$.items[0].Name")` are different expressions, because JSON keys are case-sensitive. Asserting `jsonPath("$.items").value("mug")` against a JSON array that holds several values produces a confusing failure, because `.value(...)` expects the path to resolve to a single scalar, not a collection. Use `jsonPath("$.items[0]").value("mug")` or `jsonPath("$.items", hasItem("mug"))`, depending on what you mean. When an `andExpect(...)` fails, MockMvc's message is verbose on purpose: it includes the request that was sent and the response that came back. Read it in full, because the response body often reveals the real cause (a validation error you didn't expect, an exception message from a gap in your `@ExceptionHandler`s) faster than the assertion alone.

examples.title: A GET Request With Nested jsonPath Assertions
examples.explanation: The test stubs orderService.findById(1L) to return a fully populated Order, then sends a GET request through DispatcherServlet using MockMvc. The chained andExpect() calls assert in increasing detail: a 200 status, the Content-Type header (confirming Jackson's converter was selected), a top-level field value, an array's length, and one array element. If any assertion in the chain fails, MockMvc stops there and reports that failure along with the full response, so you can see what the controller returned versus what was expected.

examples.title: A POST Request Triggering Validation, Asserting on the Error Body
examples.explanation: This test never stubs orderService.create(...), because the request should be rejected before the controller's own logic, and therefore the service, is reached. @Valid triggers Bean Validation on the deserialized CreateOrderRequest, a blank customerName fails @NotBlank, and the @RestControllerAdvice's MethodArgumentNotValidException handler produces the 400 with a structured error body, as covered in the Building REST APIs module. verifyNoInteractions(orderService) makes that expectation explicit and fails the test if the controller somehow called the service anyway, a regression that jsonPath assertions on the response alone might miss.

examples.title: Verifying a Service Was Called With the Right Arguments
examples.explanation: Besides checking the HTTP response, this test verifies that OrderController deserialized the incoming JSON correctly and passed a populated CreateOrderRequest to orderService.create(...). argThat(...) inspects the argument's fields instead of requiring object equality, which matters because CreateOrderRequest may not override equals(). Asserting the HTTP-facing response AND verifying the collaborator call is a common, thorough controller-test pattern: the response assertions confirm what the client sees, and verify() confirms the controller did the right thing internally to produce it.

misconceptions.description: Because MockMvc doesn't open a real network socket, it doesn't really test Spring's request-handling logic -- it's closer to calling the controller method directly.
misconceptions.clarification: MockMvc dispatches the simulated request through the same DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, argument resolvers, HttpMessageConverters and @ExceptionHandler machinery a real HTTP request goes through. Only the transport is simulated (no real socket, no real servlet container). Calling a controller method directly with new OrderController(mockService).getOrder(1L) bypasses all of that (no routing, no @PathVariable binding, no JSON conversion, no validation, no exception translation) and misses a whole class of bugs (a wrong mapping path, a missing @Valid, a broken @ExceptionHandler) that a MockMvc test catches because it runs the real dispatch pipeline.

misconceptions.description: You can only use MockMvc inside a @WebMvcTest -- getting a MockMvc instance requires that specific slice.
misconceptions.clarification: @WebMvcTest is the most common way to get an autowired MockMvc, because it is configured and ready out of the box. MockMvc is also available inside a full @SpringBootTest with webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.MOCK (the default when webEnvironment isn't specified) if you add @AutoConfigureMockMvc and autowire it the same way. It can even be built by hand outside any Spring test context with MockMvcBuilders.standaloneSetup(new OrderController(fakeService)).build(), a lighter test that skips Spring's context and wires up just that one controller.
misconceptions.fact: @WebMvcTest is the most common way to get an autowired MockMvc instance, because it is configured and ready to use out of the box.

exercises.prompt: This test fails with status 415 (Unsupported Media Type) instead of the expected 201, even though the JSON payload itself is well-formed and matches CreateOrderRequest exactly. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Spring MVC needs to know what format the request body is in before it can pick an HttpMessageConverter to read it -- where does that information normally come from?
Compare this request-building chain to one that successfully posts JSON elsewhere in the test suite -- what call is present there but missing here?
The fix does not involve the JSON content at all -- it involves declaring the request's Content-Type header explicitly on the MockMvc request builder.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original request supplies a body with .content(...) but never declares a Content-Type. Without one, Spring MVC can't select the HttpMessageConverter to read the body, and @RequestBody resolution fails before the controller's logic (or any JSON shape or validation issue) is considered, producing 415 Unsupported Media Type: a transport-level rejection, not a data problem. Adding .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON) declares the body's format, so Spring MVC selects the Jackson converter and the request proceeds normally.

exercises.prompt: Write a @WebMvcTest for a GET /api/products/{id} endpoint. ProductController depends on a ProductService with a method findById(Long) that returns a Product(Long id, String name, BigDecimal price). Stub the service to return a Product with id=5, name="Desk Lamp", price=29.99, then assert the response is 200 OK with the correct name and price in the JSON body.
hints: Use given(productService.findById(5L)).willReturn(...) (BDDMockito style) or when(...).thenReturn(...) to stub the mocked service before performing the request.
jsonPath("$.price") will resolve to a numeric JSON value -- compare it with .value(29.99) (a Double/number literal), not a String.
Don't forget the leading $ and dot syntax for jsonPath expressions -- $.name and $.price for top-level fields on the response object.
exercises.solutionExplanation: given(productService.findById(5L)).willReturn(...) stubs the mocked ProductService so that when the controller calls it with 5L (taken from the {id} path variable), it returns a populated Product instead of null. mockMvc.perform(get("/api/products/5")) sends the simulated request through the real DispatcherServlet and HandlerMapping, which routes it to ProductController's handler, binds 5 to the Long parameter, and calls the mocked service. The response, serialized by the real Jackson converter, is asserted field by field with jsonPath, confirming the status code and that the controller passed the service's data through into the JSON body.

assessments.prompt: What is the most accurate description of what MockMvc simulates when a test calls mockMvc.perform(get("/api/orders/1"))?
options: It replaces the controller with a Mockito-generated stub that returns a hardcoded response.
It sends a genuine HTTP request over the loopback network interface to a lightweight, temporary embedded server.
It sends the request through the real DispatcherServlet, HandlerMapping, argument resolvers, and HttpMessageConverters.
It calls the matching controller method directly via reflection, bypassing DispatcherServlet and HandlerMapping entirely.
assessments.explanation: MockMvc dispatches the simulated request through Spring MVC's real machinery end to end: routing, binding, conversion, validation and exception handling all run. The only simplification is that no real network socket or servlet container thread is involved. The “It calls the matching controller method directly…” option is wrong because routing and binding happen through HandlerMapping and argument resolvers, not direct reflection. The “It sends a genuine HTTP request over…” option describes what TestRestTemplate or WebTestClient do against a real embedded server (as with @SpringBootTest's RANDOM_PORT), not MockMvc. The “It replaces the controller with a Mockito-generated…” option is wrong because the controller is real and unmocked; only its dependencies (like a @Service) are mocked, and only if you do so.

assessments.prompt: A test writes `jsonPath("$.items").value("mug")` against a response whose items field is a JSON array containing several strings, one of which is "mug". What happens?
options: The assertion fails or produces a confusing type-mismatch error.
The assertion silently passes regardless of the array's actual contents, because a path with no index is treated as an automatic wildcard match.
The assertion passes, because .value(...) automatically checks whether the given value is present anywhere in the array.
Spring MVC automatically converts the array into just its first element before the comparison runs.
assessments.explanation: Asserting .value(...) against a jsonPath expression that resolves to an array of several values, instead of a single scalar, produces a confusing failure, because .value(...) expects a scalar match. The two corrections are indexing into a specific element (jsonPath("$.items[0]").value("mug")) or using a Hamcrest membership matcher on the whole collection (jsonPath("$.items", hasItem("mug"))), depending on the intent. The “The assertion passes, because .value(...) automatically checks…”, “The assertion silently passes regardless…” and “Spring MVC automatically converts the array into…” options each describe forgiving behavior that jsonPath's .value(...) does not provide.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes MockMvc from TestRestTemplate/WebTestClient?
options: MockMvc and TestRestTemplate are functionally identical; choosing between them is purely a matter of style.
MockMvc only supports GET requests -- POST, PUT, and DELETE require switching to TestRestTemplate.
TestRestTemplate cannot handle JSON responses at all, only plain text bodies.

TestRestTemplate/WebTestClient fire genuine HTTP requests at a real, running embedded server (typically paired with @SpringBootTest's RANDOM_PORT), exercising the whole stack including real network serialization; MockMvc simulates the same dispatch entirely in memory, with no real socket, testing the web layer's logic without paying for a network round trip.
assessments.explanation: TestRestTemplate and WebTestClient are end-to-end tools that need a real running server (the RANDOM_PORT style of @SpringBootTest from the previous concept), while MockMvc simulates the same dispatch machinery with no real socket, at close to unit-test speed. The “MockMvc and TestRestTemplate are functionally identical; choosing…” option collapses a distinction that matters when choosing between them. The “MockMvc only supports GET requests -- POST…” option is false: MockMvc supports post(...), put(...) and delete(...) through MockMvcRequestBuilders, as the examples show. The “TestRestTemplate cannot handle JSON responses at all…” option is false: TestRestTemplate handles JSON as readily as MockMvc.

assessments.prompt: A response body contains the JSON key "customerName", but a test asserts `jsonPath("$.CustomerName").value("Amy")` (capital C). What happens?
options: Spring MVC normalizes JSON key casing automatically before any jsonPath expression is evaluated against the response.

The assertion fails to find a matching value, because JSON keys -- and therefore the JSONPath expressions that navigate them -- are case-sensitive; $.CustomerName does not refer to the same field as $.customerName.
The test fails to compile, because jsonPath expressions are validated against the target DTO class's exact field names at compile time.
The assertion passes, because JSONPath expressions are case-insensitive by default when matching JSON keys.
assessments.explanation: JSON keys are case-sensitive and jsonPath navigates them literally, so $.items[0].name and $.items[0].Name are different expressions, and $.CustomerName does not refer to the field $.customerName. The “The assertion passes, because JSONPath expressions…” and “Spring MVC normalizes JSON key casing automatically…” options both invent a normalization step that doesn't exist. The “The test fails to compile, because jsonPath…” option is wrong: jsonPath expressions are plain strings evaluated at runtime against the parsed response, with no compile-time check against a DTO's field names.

assessments.prompt: Explain, end to end, what happens when a MockMvc test calls mockMvc.perform(post(...).contentType(...).content(...)) against a @WebMvcTest-loaded controller that has a @MockBean service dependency, through to the final assertions.
assessments.modelAnswer: When perform(...) is called, MockMvc hands the simulated request to the real DispatcherServlet loaded in the @WebMvcTest context, as a genuine HTTP request would be handled in production, except that it never travels over a socket. DispatcherServlet consults the HandlerMapping built at context startup to find the controller method whose path pattern and HTTP method match, and uses the declared Content-Type to choose an HttpMessageConverter able to read the body (for JSON, the autoconfigured Jackson converter). That converter deserializes the bytes into the @RequestBody parameter's Java type, populating its fields from the JSON. If @Valid is present, Bean Validation then runs against that object, and a violation short-circuits everything after it, routing to whatever @ExceptionHandler is registered for validation failures. If validation passes, the controller method runs, and because its @Service dependency was registered as a @MockBean, any call into that service returns whatever was stubbed with given(...)/when(...), or Mockito's default (null, 0, or an empty collection) if nothing was stubbed for that call. Whatever the controller returns is passed back through the Jackson converter in reverse and serialized into the JSON response body that the andExpect(...) assertions inspect with status(), jsonPath(...) and similar matchers. Every step runs real Spring MVC code (routing, conversion, validation, serialization), which is why a MockMvc test is a meaningful test of the web layer's behavior and not just a check that a method returns a value.

concepts.title: Mocking Dependencies with @MockBean
concepts.description: @MockBean replaces a real bean in the Spring test context with a Mockito mock, letting a test isolate the component it cares about from its collaborators. The replacement has consequences for what gets stubbed, what silently returns null, and how well the suite can reuse cached contexts.
learningObjectives: Explain what @MockBean does to the Spring test ApplicationContext, and how that differs from a plain Mockito mock created with @Mock or mock(...).
Stub a @MockBean's behavior with when(...).thenReturn(...) (or given(...).willReturn(...)) and verify interactions with verify(...).
Predict what an unstubbed @MockBean method call returns for object, primitive, and collection return types.
Explain why adding or removing a @MockBean can force Spring's test-context cache to build a brand-new context, and the performance implication of that.
Choose correctly between @MockBean and a hand-constructed fake for a given testing scenario.

sections.heading: What @MockBean Actually Replaces
sections.body:
`@MockBean`, applied to a field in a Spring test class, does two things: it creates a Mockito mock of the declared type, and it registers that mock *in the test's ApplicationContext*, replacing any real bean of that type (or supplying one, in a slice like `@WebMvcTest` where no real bean of that type would have been registered). Every other bean in that context that depends on the type, most often a controller depending on a service, receives the mock when the container wires it, as it would a real bean.

This differs from a plain Mockito mock created with `@Mock` (under `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`) or `mock(SomeType.class)`. A plain mock is an object you construct and wire in yourself, with no Spring container involved, which suits a pure unit test of a class built with `new OrderService(mockRepository)`. `@MockBean` is for when *Spring's container* constructs the object under test (a controller inside a `@WebMvcTest`, say) and you need the container to hand it a mock, because you have no `new` call of your own to pass one into.

A version note: Spring Boot 3.4 deprecated `@MockBean` and `@SpyBean` in favor of Spring Framework 6.2's `@MockitoBean` and `@MockitoSpyBean` (package `org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito`), and Spring Boot 4 removes the old annotations. They work the same way for this lesson's purposes, and the examples use `@MockBean`, so on Boot 3.4 or later substitute the new annotation. One restriction: `@MockitoBean` can be placed on test-class fields but not in `@Configuration` classes.

sections.heading: Stubbing and Verifying
sections.body: Once a `@MockBean` is registered, it behaves like an ordinary Mockito mock. `given(mockedService.findById(1L)).willReturn(order)` (BDDMockito style) or `when(mockedService.findById(1L)).thenReturn(order)` (plain Mockito style) sets what the mock returns for that call, and `willThrow(...)`/`thenThrow(...)` makes it throw instead, which is how you test a controller's handling of a service failure. After the code under test has run, `verify(mockedService).findById(1L)` asserts that `findById` was called with that argument; `verify(mockedService, times(2))....` asserts an exact call count; and `verify(mockedService).save(argThat(order -> order.getCustomerName().equals("Amy")))` verifies a call with an argument matching a predicate, useful when the passed object has no meaningful `equals()`.

sections.heading: Default Mock Behavior and the Silent Null Trap
sections.body:
When a `@MockBean`'s method is called *without* having been stubbed for that call, Mockito does **not** throw an exception to flag it. It returns a type-appropriate default (Mockito's `RETURNS_DEFAULTS` answer): `null` for most object return types, including `String`; `0`/`0.0`/`false` for primitives; an empty, non-null collection for `List`, `Set` and `Map`; and `Optional.empty()` for `Optional`.

This is a common, quiet source of test bugs. If you stub `orderService.findById(1L)` but the controller under test calls `orderService.findById(2L)` (perhaps because of a real bug, such as extracting the wrong path variable), the mock doesn't complain about an argument it wasn't told to expect. It returns `null` for the unstubbed call, and the resulting `NullPointerException` (if the controller then calls a method on that `null`) can look like an unrelated bug when the real problem is a mismatch between what you stubbed and what was called. A real bean that was missing would produce a `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` or a meaningful domain exception; an unstubbed mock fails silently and generically, which is why you should stub every call path a test exercises, not only the happy path you're focused on.

sections.heading: @MockBean and Context Caching
sections.body:
As covered in this module's first concept, Spring's test framework caches a built `ApplicationContext` and reuses it across test classes that request an identical configuration, to avoid paying a context's startup cost for every class. The set of `@MockBean`s declared on a test class is part of that configuration's cache key: two classes that are otherwise identical but declare *different* sets of mocked beans ask the cache for two different contexts, and each gets its own freshly built one.

A codebase where every test class mocks a slightly different, ad hoc combination of dependencies defeats context caching far more often than one where test classes covering the same layer mock the same shared set of collaborators (often by extending a common base test class that declares the standard `@MockBean`s for that layer). That is not a reason to avoid `@MockBean`, which remains the right tool for isolating a component. It is a reason to keep the mocked set within a test class deliberate and, where reasonable, consistent with sibling classes, instead of mocking an arbitrary, changing subset per test method.

examples.title: Stubbing a @MockBean's Return Value
examples.explanation: @MockBean registers a Mockito mock as the OrderService bean inside this @WebMvcTest context, so OrderController's constructor is satisfied with the mock instead of a real service. given(...).willReturn(...) stubs one call, findById(1L), and the controller's real routing and JSON serialization determine what ends up in the HTTP response from whatever the mock returns. verify(orderService).findById(1L) is a separate assertion from the jsonPath checks: it confirms the controller called the service with the expected argument, instead of only checking that the response looked right.

examples.title: Verifying Interactions and Argument Matching
examples.explanation: times(1) makes the expected call count explicit, though a bare verify(...) also defaults to exactly once. It is useful when the point of a test is that a side-effecting operation like a delete happens exactly once, not zero times and not twice. The second verify, with never() and an argThat predicate for any id other than 42, is a negative assertion: it fails if the controller called deleteById with a different id at any point, catching a wrong implementation that checking only the positive case might miss.

examples.title: The Silent-Null Trap From an Unstubbed Call
examples.explanation: This example is about what goes wrong, not a passing test. The mock was stubbed only for findById(1L), so a controller bug that calls findById(0L) gets Mockito's default of null for that unstubbed call, with no exception and no warning. The NullPointerException happens later, wherever the controller or the JSON serializer uses that null Order, which can be some distance from the real defect. The procedural lesson: when a MockMvc test fails with an unexpected 500 instead of a clean assertion failure, check whether every call the code under test makes was stubbed, not just the one you assumed it would make.

misconceptions.description: @MockBean is exactly the same as a plain Mockito @Mock or mock(...) call -- just a different-sounding annotation for creating a mock object.
misconceptions.clarification: Both create a Mockito mock underneath, but @MockBean also registers that mock in Spring's ApplicationContext, replacing (or supplying) the bean of that type for every other bean the container wires. That only makes sense when Spring's container constructs the object under test. A plain @Mock or mock(...) produces an object you wire in yourself, outside any Spring container, which suits a pure unit test built with `new`. Using @MockBean when no Spring context is involved is unnecessary; using a plain Mockito mock when the container must inject it into a bean it constructs (like a controller in a @WebMvcTest) doesn't work, since there's no `new` call of your own to hand the mock to.

misconceptions.description: If you forget to stub a @MockBean's method before it gets called during a test, Mockito throws an exception to warn you that the call was unexpected.
misconceptions.clarification: Mockito's default for an unstubbed mock method is lenient, not strict: it returns null for most object return types (String included), the zero-equivalent (0, 0.0, false) for primitives, an empty collection for List, Set and Map, and Optional.empty() for Optional, with no exception and no warning. That is why an unstubbed call the test didn't anticipate tends to surface later as a confusing NullPointerException downstream, instead of an immediate, clearly labeled failure at the point of the unexpected call.

exercises.prompt: This test fails with a NullPointerException thrown from inside OrderController, not from the test method itself. Given that OrderController.getOrder(id) calls orderService.findById(id) and then calls .getCustomerName() on the result, find and fix the bug in the test.
hints: Look carefully at the id used in the stub (given(orderService.findById(2L))) versus the id in the actual request path (/api/orders/1).
The mock was only told what to do for findById(2L). What does it do when the controller actually calls findById(1L) instead?
Fix either the stub's argument or the request path so they refer to the same order id -- they currently disagree.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The request hits GET /api/orders/1, so the controller calls orderService.findById(1L), but the stub was written for findById(2L), a different, unstubbed call as far as Mockito is concerned. Because Mockito returns null for an unstubbed call instead of throwing or warning, findById(1L) returned null, and the controller's call to .getCustomerName() on that null Order threw the NullPointerException the test observed, nowhere near the assertion lines, which never got to run. Changing the stub to findById(1L), to match the request, lets the mock answer the call the controller makes, so the rest of the test runs and asserts as intended.

exercises.prompt: Given a @MockBean InventoryService inventoryService with no stubbing configured for any of its methods, what does each of these calls return, and why don't any of them throw an exception?
exercises.code:
// No when(...)/given(...) stubbing has been set up for inventoryService at all.

Integer count = inventoryService.getStockCount("WIDGET");     // int return type
String name = inventoryService.getProductName("WIDGET");      // String return type
boolean inStock = inventoryService.isInStock("WIDGET");        // boolean return type
List<String> tags = inventoryService.getTags("WIDGET");        // List<String> return type
hints: Mockito's default, unstubbed behavior differs by the DECLARED RETURN TYPE of the method, not by whether the method 'makes sense' to call.
Primitive return types (int, boolean) have a natural zero-equivalent default; reference types like String default to something else entirely.
Mockito's default answer returns an empty collection for common collection return types such as List, Set and Map, instead of null.
exercises.expectedAnswer: count is 0 (int's default), name is null (String is a reference type with no stubbing), inStock is false (boolean's default), and tags is an empty List (Mockito's default for collection return types). None of these calls throws, because Mockito's default answer for an unstubbed mock method is a lenient, type-appropriate default value, not an exception.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Mockito gives every unstubbed mock method a default answer that depends on the method's declared return type. For primitive numeric and boolean return types it is the natural zero-equivalent (0 for getStockCount's int, false for isInStock's boolean), because a primitive can't be null. For an ordinary reference type like String, with no special-cased default, the answer is null. For List, Set and Map, Mockito's default answer (RETURNS_DEFAULTS, which delegates to ReturnsEmptyValues) returns an empty, non-null collection, which spares you a common NullPointerException when calling .size() or iterating an unstubbed result. None of these calls throws, which is the behavior to remember: an unanticipated call to a @MockBean fails quietly, by returning something plausible-looking, not loudly.

assessments.prompt: A @MockBean UserRepository has no stubbing configured for its findByEmail(String) method, which returns Optional<User>. A test calls repository.findByEmail("amy@example.com") without stubbing it first. What is returned?
options: The method throws NullPointerException immediately, because Mockito requires every mock method to be explicitly stubbed before it's called in a test.
The test fails to compile, because calling an unstubbed mock method is a Mockito error caught at compile time.
A real UserRepository bean is used instead, since @MockBean falls back to the actual implementation for unstubbed methods.
An empty Optional (Optional.empty()), because Mockito's default answer recognizes Optional as a special case and avoids returning a bare null for it.
assessments.explanation: Mockito's default answer has a special case for Optional-returning methods: instead of a bare null (an easy source of confusing NullPointerExceptions, given how often Optional is chained with .map()/.orElse()), an unstubbed method returning Optional gives Optional.empty(). The “The method throws NullPointerException immediately, because Mockito…” option is wrong: Mockito never requires stubbing before a call and always has a default answer. The “A real UserRepository bean is used instead…” option is wrong: @MockBean fully replaces the real bean, with no fallback to the real implementation for unstubbed calls. The “The test fails to compile, because calling…” option is wrong: neither Mockito nor the compiler can detect an unstubbed call statically, so it is purely runtime behavior.

assessments.prompt: A pure unit test constructs `OrderService service = new OrderService(mockRepository);` directly, with no Spring container involved anywhere in the test. What is the more appropriate way to create mockRepository, and why?
options: Either approach works identically, since @MockBean is simply a more verbose alias for a plain mock(...) call.

A plain Mockito mock, created via @Mock or mock(OrderRepository.class), because no Spring container is constructing OrderService here -- the mock just needs to be an ordinary Java object handed directly into the constructor, and @MockBean's whole reason for existing (registering into an ApplicationContext) has nothing to attach to.
Neither -- OrderRepository must be a genuine bean retrieved from a real ApplicationContext for this test to be considered valid.
@MockBean, since it is always the preferred, more modern replacement for creating any mock in a Spring Boot codebase.
assessments.explanation: The deciding factor is who constructs the object under test. Here the test calls `new OrderService(...)` itself, so no Spring container exists for @MockBean's context registration to act on, and a plain Mockito mock is just an ordinary object the test passes in by hand. The “@MockBean, since it is always the preferred…” option overgeneralizes @MockBean to a situation where it gives no benefit. The “Either approach works identically, since @MockBean…” option is false: @MockBean does extra work (registering in an ApplicationContext) that a plain mock doesn't, though both are Mockito mocks underneath. The “Neither -- OrderRepository must be a genuine…” option invents a requirement that contradicts the point of a Spring-free unit test.

assessments.prompt: A @MockBean has three unstubbed methods: getTags() returning List<String>, getDescription() returning String, and isActive() returning boolean. Which of these calls is most likely to eventually cause a NullPointerException downstream, if the calling code doesn't explicitly check for null first?
options: getTags(), because Mockito returns a bare null for List return types, exactly like any other reference type.
isActive(), because Mockito cannot produce a default value for a primitive boolean return type and throws an exception instead.
getDescription(), because String has no special-cased default in Mockito's default answer, so it returns null.
None of them -- Mockito always throws UnsupportedStubbingException for any call that wasn't explicitly stubbed.
assessments.explanation: Mockito's default answer is type-aware: List and other common collection types get an empty, non-null collection, and primitives like boolean have a zero-equivalent (false), but an ordinary reference type like String has no special case and defaults to null, which is the value most likely to blow up later if code calls a method on it without a null check. The “getTags(), because Mockito returns a bare null…” option applies the plain-reference-type default to List, which Mockito handles specially. The “isActive(), because Mockito cannot produce a default…” option invents an exception Mockito doesn't throw for primitives. The “None of them -- Mockito always throws…” option is false: for unstubbed calls Mockito returns a default value instead of throwing.

assessments.prompt: Two @WebMvcTest classes test different controllers but declare the exact same set of @MockBean types. A third test class in the same slice adds one additional @MockBean beyond what the other two declare. What is the effect on Spring's test-context caching?
options: The first two test classes' identical configuration lets them share one cached context.
Declaring any @MockBean at all permanently disables context caching for the remainder of the test run.
Spring merges all three test classes' configurations into one shared context containing every @MockBean declared across all of them.
All three test classes always share a single cached context regardless of their declared @MockBean sets, simply because they're all @WebMvcTest.
assessments.explanation: The set of @MockBean types declared on a test class is part of the configuration's cache key. Two classes with identical mocked sets can share a cached context, but a class declaring even one more mocked bean requests a different configuration and gets its own newly built context. The “All three test classes always share…” option ignores that cache keys are configuration-specific, not just annotation-specific. The “Declaring any @MockBean at all permanently disables…” option overstates the effect: @MockBean doesn't disable caching, it just requires an exact match for reuse. The “Spring merges all three test classes' configurations…” option describes merging that Spring's context cache doesn't do; contexts are reused whole when identical and never combined.

assessments.prompt: A teammate is confused about when to reach for @MockBean versus a plain Mockito mock created with new MockitoAnnotations/@Mock in a test with no Spring involved at all. Explain the distinction, and also explain the 'silent null' risk that comes with using any Mockito mock, @MockBean or not.
assessments.modelAnswer: The deciding question is who constructs the object under test. If the test builds it directly, with `new SomeService(dependencyA, dependencyB)`, the test decides what to pass for each dependency, and a plain Mockito mock, created with @Mock (with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)) or mock(SomeType.class), is the right tool: no Spring container is involved, and the mock is an ordinary object handed to the constructor. @MockBean solves a different problem: it is for when SPRING's container constructs the object under test, most commonly a controller inside a @WebMvcTest, which the container builds by inspecting its constructor and injecting beans for each parameter. The test has no `new` call of its own to pass a plain mock to, so @MockBean tells the container to register a mock as the bean of that type, and it is wired into the controller (or any other Spring-managed bean that depends on it) like a real bean. (On Spring Boot 3.4 and later, @MockitoBean is the non-deprecated equivalent.) Whichever mechanism produced the mock, the same risk applies. Mockito's default for any call that wasn't stubbed is a type-appropriate value: null for most object types, a primitive's zero-equivalent for primitives, empty collections or Optional.empty() for several well-known container types. It does not throw to flag an unanticipated call. A mismatch between what the test stubbed and what the code under test calls (a wrong argument, an extra invocation) therefore doesn't fail at the point of the mismatch; it produces a plausible default that often causes a visible failure later, once something uses that value in a way a null or a zero doesn't tolerate, frequently a NullPointerException some distance from the root cause. The practical takeaway is to stub every call path the code under test exercises, not only the one the author had in mind, and to treat an unexpected NullPointerException from inside the code under test (rather than from the test's own assertions) as a hint to check whether a mock call matches what was stubbed.
